steps.say: Thoracic outlet syndrome encompasses symptoms caused by compression of neurovascular structures passing from the neck to the axilla. The scalene triangle is bordered by the anterior scalene muscle, middle scalene muscle, and first rib. It holds and transmits the brachial plexus trunks and subclavian artery.
steps.tx: Thoracic outlet syndrome arises from dynamic extrinsic compression of the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels within three confined anatomical spaces. The **scalene triangle**, bounded by the **anterior scalene muscle**, middle scalene, and the **first rib**, contains the brachial trunks and subclavian artery.

nodes.label: Cervical nerve roots C5-T1 exit neural foramina
Passage through interscalene triangle over first rib
Traverse costoclavicular space beneath subclavius muscle
Enter retropectoral minor space into the upper arm

steps.say: Thoracic outlet syndrome is categorized into three distinct clinical forms. Neurogenic syndrome accounts for over ninety percent of cases, causing upper extremity pain, numbness, and paresthesias. Venous thoracic outlet syndrome, or Paget-Schroetter syndrome, causes acute arm swelling, while arterial compression causes digital ischemia.
steps.tx: Thoracic outlet syndrome is classified into three clinical subtypes. **Neurogenic TOS** accounts for over 90 percent of cases, presenting with paresthesias and pain. **Venous TOS** presents with sudden axillosubclavian thrombosis, while rare **arterial TOS** causes upper extremity claudication and digital microembolism.

rows: Ulnar paresthesias, medial arm aching, Gilliatt-Sumner hand wasting
Acute dominant arm cyanosis, severe swelling, prominent chest veins
Subclavian aneurysm, distal thromboembolism, digital pallor and ischemia

steps.say: Physical examination provokes symptoms by narrowing the thoracic outlet. The elevated arm stress test, or Roos test, reproduces aching and paresthesias within three minutes. The Adson test detects subclavian compression by monitoring radial pulse dampening during deep inspiration and neck rotation.
steps.tx: Diagnostic evaluation utilizes provocative maneuvers that exacerbate neurovascular compression. The **Roos test** reproduces forearm aching and paresthesias within three minutes of 90-degree abduction. The **Adson test** monitors obliteration of the **radial pulse dampening** during neck extension and ipsilateral head rotation.

left.title: Roos Elevated Arm Stress Test
points: Arms abducted 90 degrees with continuous hand gripping
Inability to sustain 3 minutes due to pain and fatigue
Highly sensitive clinical test for neurogenic compression

right.title: Adson Provocative Maneuver
points: Neck extended and rotated toward symptomatic side with deep breath
Monitors reduction or loss of radial pulse amplitude
Evaluates scalene triangle narrowing and arterial compression

steps.say: Bony anomalies such as cervical ribs and elongated transverse processes are major structural etiologies. A complete or incomplete cervical rib arises from the seventh cervical vertebra, narrowing the scalene space. Congenital fibrous bands extending from the cervical rib compress the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.
steps.tx: Congenital skeletal anomalies predispose to severe thoracic outlet entrapment. A complete **cervical rib** arising from the C7 vertebra or a rigid fibrous band elevates and compresses the brachial plexus lower trunk and subclavian artery, precipitating post-stenotic dilation and **bony compression**.

nodes.label: Congenital presence of C7 cervical rib or fibrous band
Elevation and anterior displacement of brachial trunks
Repetitive mechanical friction during arm abduction
Axonal demyelination or post-stenotic arterial aneurysm

steps.tx: Follow the extra rib in the illustration from the seventh cervical vertebra to where it meets the first rib below. That bony bridge lifts and narrows the outlet, pressing the subclavian artery and the **lower trunk** of the brachial plexus against unyielding structures. The anatomy explains the mixed picture clinicians see: vascular signs in the hand alongside wasting and sensory change in a medial forearm and hand distribution.
steps.say: A complete cervical rib compresses the subclavian artery and lower brachial plexus trunk at the thoracic outlet. Vascular and medial hand neurological signs follow.

steps.say: Venous thoracic outlet syndrome, also known as Paget-Schroetter syndrome, represents effort thrombosis of the subclavian vein. Repetitive vigorous overhead arm movements compress the vein between the subclavius muscle, clavicle, and first rib. Endothelial injury causes acute extensive thrombosis.
steps.tx: Venous TOS, or **Paget-Schroetter syndrome**, presents as acute **effort thrombosis** of the axillosubclavian vein following repetitive overhead exertion. The vein suffers repeated crushing between the first rib and **subclavius muscle**, causing intimal inflammation, fibrosis, and acute extensive thrombosis. Emergency clinical presentation demands prompt diagnostic duplex sonography and catheter venography to establish the full extent of venous obstruction.

left.title: Paget-Schroetter Effort Thrombosis
points: Young, muscular athletes engaging in overhead sports
Mechanical compression between subclavius and first rib
Requires urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis and rib excision

right.title: Secondary Upper Extremity DVT
points: Related to indwelling central lines, pacemakers, or ports
Underlying foreign body thrombogenesis and endothelial stasis
Managed primarily with systemic anticoagulation without surgery

steps.tx: Contrast in this venogram stops abruptly where the vein passes the crowded costoclavicular space, then reappears through a tangle of shoulder collaterals. That pattern is effort related **axillosubclavian thrombosis** in a young active patient rather than a line associated clot. The collateral network proves the obstruction is haemodynamically important, and management pairs early thrombus clearance with later decompression of the outlet so recurrence is less likely.
steps.say: The venogram shows axillosubclavian effort thrombosis with shoulder collaterals bypassing the costoclavicular obstruction. Treatment combines thrombus clearance with later outlet decompression.

vis.alt: Upper limb venogram with axillosubclavian effort thrombosis and collateral veins around the shoulder
vis.caption: An upper limb venogram shows axillosubclavian effort thrombosis with collateral veins around the shoulder. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Management of Paget-Schroetter syndrome follows a multidisciplinary protocol. Clinicians initiate urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis to clear thrombus and restore vein patency. Prompt surgical resection of the first rib within two to six weeks relieves mechanical compression, preventing recurrent thrombosis.
steps.tx: Modern management of acute venous TOS mandates emergency **catheter-directed thrombolysis** to achieve complete clot clearance. Once vein patency is restored, surgical **first rib resection** is performed during the index admission to eliminate the extrinsic bone compression and prevent **recurrent thrombosis**.

nodes.label: Acute arm swelling: perform duplex ultrasound and venogram
Catheter-directed tPA infusion to lyse acute vein clot
Confirm vein patency and demonstrate costoclavicular pinch
Perform prompt surgical first rib resection to prevent recurrence

steps.say: Surgical decompression removes the bony floor of the thoracic outlet. The transaxillary approach provides cosmetic exposure for complete first rib resection and cervical rib removal. Alternatively, the supraclavicular approach provides excellent visualization for neurogenic decompression and brachial plexus neurolysis.
steps.tx: Surgical decompression involves **first rib resection** combined with anterior and middle **scalene muscle release**. The cosmetic **transaxillary approach** provides an incision for total rib removal, while the supraclavicular exposure allows wide direct visualization for comprehensive brachial plexus neurolysis and fibrous band excision.

rows: Venous TOS and routine first rib resection
Direct access to entire rib length; hidden axillary scar
Neurogenic TOS with cervical rib / fibrous bands
Direct visualization of roots C5-T1 and brachial neurolysis
Direct exposure of subclavian vein and subclavius tendon

steps.say: First rib resection demands meticulous surgical dissection to prevent iatrogenic nerve injury. Retraction or transection can injure the long thoracic nerve, causing a winged scapula. Damage to the phrenic nerve produces hemidiaphragmatic paralysis, while traction on the lower trunk causes permanent hand numbness.
steps.tx: Iatrogenic complications during first rib resection demand extreme vigilance. Traction or transection of the **long thoracic nerve** produces a debilitating **winged scapula**, while dividing the **phrenic nerve** causes hemidiaphragmatic paralysis, and stretch injury to the lower trunk causes permanent hand dysfunction.

rows: Serratus anterior paralysis causing winged scapula
Ulnar sensory loss and intrinsic hand muscle wasting
